solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Showing some front — or rear? (6)

blocks.note: front as nerve or brass neck: showing it is being impudent
the saucy second reading: a bare rear shows its two halves

annotation.surface: Someone baring a little too much, whichever side is facing you.
annotation.walkthrough: Front here is nerve, the kind a cheeky person shows; the tag 'or rear?' then offers the bottom's cheeks as a second, saucier reading of the same word.
annotation.definitionFit: Impudence is called front or brass, and buttocks are cheeks, so one word covers both the attitude and the view from behind.

entries.clue: Nurse pulled up underwear in time (7)

indicatorNotes.pulled up: in a down clue, pulling something up makes it read bottom to top
indicatorNotes.in: the underwear sits inside the time

blocks.note: an hour is a unit of time
a bra is underwear; turned upward it reads ARB

annotation.surface: A nurse hurriedly hitching up her underwear before anyone sees.
annotation.walkthrough: Nurse is the verb, as in nursing or harbouring a grudge, not the hospital worker the surface shows.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym when the object is a feeling: you nurse or harbour a grudge, keeping it alive inside you.

entries.clue: Overlooking the cause of this? (9)

blocks.note: the surface sense is ignoring; the setter means looking over and over, too much
what excessive looking brings on

annotation.surface: Someone neglecting the root of a problem.
annotation.walkthrough: Overlooking seems to mean ignoring; read it as over-looking, looking too much, and the result is tired eyes.
annotation.definitionFit: Staring too long at a screen or page tires the eyes, so over-looking literally causes the ache.

entries.clue: Go on, settle up (3)

indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, up means the word reads bottom to top

blocks.note: to settle a bill is to pay it; the letters then run upward

annotation.surface: Someone urging a customer to pay the bill.
annotation.walkthrough: Go on is talking at length, not encouragement: a dog that yaps keeps going on.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal synonym: going on means talking tediously at length, the way a small dog barks without stopping.

entries.clue: In street, I mean to wait it out (3,5)

indicatorNotes.In: the I goes inside the street

blocks.note: ST is the standard abbreviation for street
I as written
tight = mean, stingy

annotation.surface: Someone out in the street explaining they plan to stay put.
annotation.walkthrough: Mean looks like the verb in 'I mean'; it is the adjective for stingy.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to stay put and do nothing until trouble passes is to wait it out.

entries.clue: Glib talk about twin cross breed of dog (8,7)

indicatorNotes.about: the glib talk goes around the other pieces

blocks.note: a spiel is a slick, glib patter
a ringer, as in dead ringer, is an exact double
to span a river is to cross it

annotation.surface: A salesman's patter about a crossbred dog with a twin.
annotation.walkthrough: Cross breed reads as a mongrel, but cross is the verb span and breed belongs to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: this gun dog, bred to spring game from cover, is one breed among many.

entries.clue: Kid angry at sailor? You can bet on it (11)

indicatorNotes.angry: angry letters are agitated, stirred up into a new order

blocks.note: a tot is a small child
these eight letters rearranged

annotation.surface: A child cross with a sailor, and a sure thing to wager on.
annotation.walkthrough: The totalisator, or tote, is the machine that pools bets at a racecourse; 'You can bet on it' sounds like a promise but is literal.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the tote is the racecourse pool system through which punters place their bets.

entries.clue: Author at home having caught disease on farm (5)

indicatorNotes.having caught: the home phrase catches the disease inside it

blocks.note: to be in is to be at home
BSE, mad cow disease, is a disease of cattle

annotation.surface: A writer at home who has picked up something nasty from livestock.
annotation.walkthrough: BSE was the British cattle epidemic of the 1980s and 90s, so it is the farm disease.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Norwegian playwright of A Doll's House and Hedda Gabler.

entries.clue: Pound end of blade into solid weapon (7)

indicatorNotes.into: the pieces before it go inside the solid
indicatorNotes.end of: take the last letter of blade

blocks.note: hard = solid
lb is the abbreviation for a pound in weight
the last letter of blade

annotation.surface: A smith hammering the tip of a blade into a sturdy weapon.
annotation.walkthrough: Pound looks like a verb for hammering; it is the unit, abbreviated LB.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: a medieval pole arm with an axe blade and spike.

entries.clue: Ariel became such a bohemian (4,6)

blocks.note: in The Tempest, the sprite Ariel is released by Prospero at the play's end
someone living an unconventional, artistic life

annotation.surface: Shakespeare's sprite turning into an unconventional artistic type.
annotation.walkthrough: The first half is literal: Ariel is a spirit bound to serve Prospero and freed at the end, so he becomes exactly what the idiom describes.
annotation.definitionFit: Ariel is literally a spirit set free, while the idiom names a person who ignores convention, like a bohemian.

entries.clue: Lawyer of singular kind (4)

blocks.note: S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular
ilk = kind, sort

annotation.surface: A one-of-a-kind lawyer.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain a senior barrister, a King's Counsel, is called a silk after the silk gown they wear.
annotation.definitionFit: British legal slang: senior counsel wear silk gowns, so taking silk means becoming a KC.

entries.clue: Laugh with companion and still drink (6)

blocks.note: a hoot is a loud laugh
CH = Companion of Honour, a British order

annotation.surface: Sharing a laugh with a friend and still having a drink.
annotation.walkthrough: Still is not 'yet' but the apparatus: the answer is liquor made in an illicit still.
annotation.definitionFit: Slang for rough home-distilled liquor, so a drink that comes out of a still.

entries.clue: Stir in? (5,6)

blocks.note: not mixing but slang for prison, as in doing time in stir
in as at home, indoors

annotation.surface: A cooking instruction to mix something in.
annotation.walkthrough: Stir is slang for prison, and 'in' means at home: a sentence served at home, not in a cell.
annotation.definitionFit: Confinement ordered by a court but served at home is prison that keeps you in.

entries.clue: One not dreaming of only the past (2,6)

blocks.note: someone who does not long for anything
true once but not any more

annotation.surface: Someone who has stopped fantasising and lives in memories.
annotation.walkthrough: The first half is a whimsical noun: a longer is one who longs, so someone not dreaming of anything is 'no longer'.
annotation.definitionFit: The phrase means not now, only formerly, and read as a noun it is a person who has stopped longing.

entries.clue: A very well rigged sail in current novel (8,6)

indicatorNotes.rigged: rigged means fixed or set up differently, so the letters are rearranged
indicatorNotes.in: the pieces before it go inside the current

blocks.note: a trend is a current of fashion or opinion
A as written
'sure!' = very well, all right
the letters of sail rearranged

annotation.surface: A well-rigged sailing ship in the flow of a story.
annotation.walkthrough: Sails, rigging and currents paint a sea story, which suits Stevenson's pirate novel; current is not the flow of water but a trend.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: Robert Louis Stevenson's 1883 pirate adventure is a novel.

entries.clue: Do one-eighty here and there in boat race (5,4)

blocks.note: about = here and there, all around
Cockney rhyming slang: boat race = face

annotation.surface: A rowing crew turning round mid-race.
annotation.walkthrough: The Boat Race is the Oxford–Cambridge rowing race, but in Cockney rhyming slang it means face.
annotation.definitionFit: A military drill command to turn and face the opposite way, used as a verb for a full reversal of direction.

entries.clue: A novelist can or might give alternative to “chatty” (14)

indicatorNotes.might give: the letters could give the answer once reordered

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters

annotation.surface: A writer searching for a synonym for chatty.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a writer at the thesaurus, and the answer is exactly what that writer might pick.
annotation.definitionFit: A near-synonym: both describe an informal, talkative style, so one can stand in for the other.

entries.clue: Stuff about Ulster by posh nutcase (7)

indicatorNotes.about: stuff goes around the other pieces

blocks.note: to cram is to stuff
NI = Northern Ireland, often called Ulster
U = upper-class, posh

annotation.surface: Talk of a well-to-do lunatic from Northern Ireland.
annotation.walkthrough: Nutcase means a madman, but read literally it is the case that holds your nut, the head.
annotation.definitionFit: Nut is slang for head, so the case around it is the skull.

entries.clue: A rocky gap, one near peak (7)

indicatorNotes.rocky: rocky means unsteady, so the letters are shaken up

blocks.note: anagram fodder: A, GAP and ONE

annotation.surface: A climber at a rocky gap, close to the summit.
annotation.walkthrough: The apogee is the farthest point of an orbit from Earth; the mountain picture disguises the astronomy.
annotation.definitionFit: The adjective from apogee, an orbit's high point, so it describes being at or near that peak.

entries.clue: Bugs Bunny’s first performance — more weird talking (8)

indicatorNotes.first: take the first letter of Bunny
indicatorNotes.talking: the word is spoken, so only its sound counts

blocks.note: the first letter of Bunny
an act is a performance
eerier = more weird; only its sound is used, spelt differently

annotation.surface: A cartoon rabbit's debut, with increasingly strange speech.
annotation.walkthrough: Bugs Bunny is one name in the surface; split it and Bugs is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal: bugs are germs, the microbes that make you ill.

entries.clue: Dance as a couple in Strictly (5)

blocks.note: an Argentine partner dance
the word Strictly holds two copies of one letter, and the radio alphabet has a code word for that letter

annotation.surface: A couple performing on Strictly Come Dancing, the BBC celebrity ballroom contest.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one pair of dancers on the show; in fact 'a couple in Strictly' is the two Ts in the word, and T is Tango in the NATO phonetic alphabet.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: the ballroom dance, and the radio code word for T, a letter that appears twice in Strictly.

entries.clue: Budget speech abandoned by leader (6)

indicatorNotes.abandoned by leader: the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: an oration is a formal speech; its first letter goes

annotation.surface: A Chancellor's Budget speech that his party leader has disowned.
annotation.walkthrough: Budget is the verb, to allocate sparingly, not the annual financial statement the surface suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: both mean to share out a limited supply in controlled amounts.

entries.clue: Character witness (4)

blocks.note: a written symbol, such as a plus or a letter
the verb: to put your name to a document as witness

annotation.walkthrough: Character is a written symbol; to witness a document is to put your name on it.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: a symbol on the page, and the act of adding your signature as witness.

entries.clue: Out. I’m not so thrilled about that (10)

indicatorNotes.about: thrilled goes around the other piece

blocks.note: elated = thrilled
not so = not out, i.e. I'M IN

annotation.surface: A contestant just knocked out, admitting they are not very pleased.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not so' refers back to the definition: I'm not out, so I'M IN.
annotation.definitionFit: In games and contests, a player knocked out of play is out.

entries.clue: Monkey, a little chimpanzee (3)

indicatorNotes.a little: only a small part of the next word is used

blocks.note: sitting inside chIMPanzee

annotation.surface: A small chimp.
annotation.walkthrough: Monkey is a mischievous child, as in 'you little monkey', not the animal.
annotation.definitionFit: A playful term for a naughty child, just as 'little monkey' is.

entries.clue: Unforgettable time in base (8)

blocks.note: base = low, immoral
T is the abbreviation for time

annotation.surface: A memorable spell spent at a military base.
annotation.walkthrough: Base is the adjective, morally low, not a camp.
annotation.definitionFit: Of fame or work that lives forever, so never forgotten, as in an immortal performance.

entries.clue: Puts down in the correct order (6)

annotation.definition: Puts down in the correct order

blocks.note: not insults or records but a bird's soft feathers, placed
tidied and arranged neatly

annotation.surface: Someone laying things out neatly in sequence.
annotation.walkthrough: Down is not a direction but soft feathers: a bird grooming with its beak puts its down in order.
annotation.definitionFit: A bird smoothing and arranging its feathers with its beak is literally setting its down straight.
